title: Ten Things: Artificial Intelligence — What Every Legal Department Really Needs to Know
pub: Ten Things You Need to Know as In-House Counsel (tenthings.blog)
author: Sterling Miller

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Miller supports the cluster’s principal proposition that legal departments are especially positioned to capture AI gains because their cost incentives favour efficiency. He also aligns with the cluster’s organisational-absorption thesis by recommending focused initial use cases, internal ownership and IT support. His evidence is mainly qualitative and predictive, and does not address later concerns about measurement, governance or market-wide outcomes.
qs: What else can AI do?**  I think the biggest impact comes from how AI is (or will be) used by in-house legal departments.
Put someone in charge of AI for the department, i.e., an AI “champion.” Their role would be to learn all there is to learn about AI and how it might best be used in the department.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s supervised, selective-deployment proposition: it recommends starting with a bounded legal-department use case, preserving escalation to a lawyer, and adding organisational complements such as internal ownership and IT support. Its predictions about job elimination are underdeveloped, and it does not substantially address verification or apprenticeship risks, but these omissions do not conflict with the cluster.
qs: Moreover, it may be possible to use AI as a “talking” FAQ service (chatbot) that can answer basic legal, HR, and compliance questions from your in-house clients, yet be “smart” enough to know when to defer the answer to a live attorney.
Find one use for AI in your legal department and start there.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s practical model of incremental, coordinated adoption within legal departments: begin with a bounded use case, assign internal ownership and involve IT in key decisions. It does not substantively address the broader claims about provider bargaining power, pricing or market restructuring, and its cost claim is predictive rather than empirical.
qs: Find one use for AI in your legal department and start there.
Make sure the colleague is part of your team dedicated to AI issues and that you bring them in on the key decisions.

st.t: Selective delegation: Rapid drafting proves little reliability
st.an: Miller directly supports selective delegation: AI handles routine, information-sifting work while lawyers retain thinking, analysis and counseling. His claims are predictive and analogy-based, so they also fit the cluster’s caution that adoption and rapid assistance do not establish reliable legal performance or net productivity gains.
qs: Put another way, “a research assistant” who can sift through the dreck and tell you what it found.
Rather, embrace it as, ultimately, it will allow you to do thing things lawyers love to do: thinking, analyzing, and counseling, while leaving the “grunt” work to the computer.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that legal AI should assist rather than replace lawyers. It requires continued lawyer involvement, human verification through independent legal analysis, and retention of professional responsibility, while envisioning AI as a research assistant for in-house counsel. It does not substantively address whether verification costs consume efficiency gains or the cluster’s confidentiality controls.
qs: **Lawyers must still stay involved and, ultimately, take whatever output from AI resources and apply good old-fashioned human legal analysis to come up with the actual legal advice.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central proposition: AI will automate selected legal tasks, alter job composition and shift lawyers toward analysis and advice rather than eliminate human legal work. It also reinforces the cluster’s qualifications that human review remains necessary and that economic value depends on implementation circumstances, while presenting employment effects and future capabilities mainly as predictions rather than established outcomes.
qs: - Jobs will be created, including managing and developing AI (legal engineers), writing algorithms for AI, and reviewing AI-assisted work product (because lawyers can never concede the final say or the provision of legal advice to AI).
The ROI of AI will be heavily fact-dependent for each organization based on what AI tools the department wants to utilize, the amount of customization needed, the number of users, and so forth.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source aligns with selective, human-led deployment: it identifies bounded operational uses and efficiency gains while insisting that lawyers interpret AI output and retain independent judgment. It also treats implementation costs, ROI, accuracy, privacy and oversight as context-dependent constraints, though several capability and employment claims are predictions rather than demonstrated findings.
qs: **Lawyers must still stay involved and, ultimately, take whatever output from AI resources and apply good old-fashioned human legal analysis to come up with the actual legal advice.
The ROI of AI will be heavily fact-dependent for each organization based on what AI tools the department wants to utilize, the amount of customization needed, the number of users, and so forth.

kp.k: AI is forecast to become an indispensable legal assistant
kp.d: Writing in August 2017, Miller predicts widespread adoption, particularly by in-house lawyers. He describes legal AI as cognitive computing that finds patterns, learns from experience and assists research, rather than presenting evidence that full professional substitution has occurred.
qs: Much like email changed the way we do business every day, AI will become ubiquitous – an indispensable assistant to practically every lawyer.
This means computers learning how to complete tasks traditionally done by people, where the focus is on looking for patterns in data, testing the data, and finding/providing results.

kp.k: In-house value combines cost savings and released lawyer capacity
kp.d: Miller argues that AI could address legal departments’ budget and manpower constraints through cheaper services and less time spent on transactional tasks. He considers the opportunity to devote existing lawyers’ time to analysis and client advice more valuable than cost reduction alone; these are prospective benefits rather than measured results.
qs: AI has the potential to solve two huge problems all legal departments face: 1) lack of budget and 2) lack of manpower.

Freeing up attorney time gives you and your business clients more access to better and more involved legal services (i.e., attorneys who can dedicate more time to thinking through problems and advising clients).

kp.k: Buyer incentives favor efficiency more strongly than law-firm incentives
kp.d: Miller expects in-house departments to drive disruption because their incentive to reduce costs is stronger than law firms’ incentive to lower prices. He frames this difference in terms of the quantity versus quality of billable hours, without quantifying adoption or predicting a specific replacement pricing model.
qs: This is true because the incentive for in-house legal departments to find the lowest cost way to do things is greater than the incentive for law firms to find ways to offer lower priced services (i.e., quantity of billable hours vs. quality of a billable hour).

kp.k: Discovery automation reduces staffing requirements without eliminating lawyers
kp.d: Miller describes a progression from keyword searches to deduplication, email-thread connection and predictive coding for context, concepts and tone. He asserts substantial time savings and reduced need for large document-review teams, but provides no comparative study or measured staffing reduction.
qs: Later, AI was used to eliminate duplicate documents and connect strings of emails, again doing in minutes that would take days if done by people.
You still need lawyers, but you no longer need an army of them.

kp.k: Diligence and contracting are targets for extensive automation
kp.d: Miller claims AI can accelerate transaction diligence traditionally undertaken by numerous outside lawyers. He also describes parameter-based contract creation, client self-service and extraction of contract information with initial setup and fine-tuning, extending automation through signature and storage. His list explicitly mixes existing and forthcoming capabilities.
qs: AI can do this in a fraction of the time.
There are AI tools that can create contracts, using whatever set of parameters the legal department feels important.

AI has progressed to the point where the entry of the key information (parties), terms, dates and other information can be done by the computer – without the need for human intervention (other than initial set up and fine tuning).

kp.k: Spend analytics could strengthen buyers’ billing negotiations
kp.d: Miller argues that AI can extract otherwise underused e-billing information to compare work and efficiency within a firm, across firms and against the wider market. He presents this as a capability that could improve legal departments’ negotiating position, not as evidence of realized fee reductions.
qs: AI provides the capability to analyze what work was done, how it aligns with other work done by that firm, how the work/efficiency compares with work provided by other firms, and how the work/efficiency compares to the market generally.
Imagine being armed with this information the next time you want to discuss billing rates with your law firms.

kp.k: Litigation prediction and misconduct detection expand analytical uses
kp.d: Miller describes litigation analytics using public court records, while expressly expressing uncertainty over whether case-fact comparison and outcome prediction are already possible or imminent. He separately asserts that AI is being used to identify bribery, fraud, compliance issues and potential litigation in corporate records, without reporting accuracy measures.
qs: It will soon be possible (or perhaps it’s already possible) to compare the facts of your case to other cases already decided by a court (or courts) and get a predictor of how your case will fare.
AI is being used to sniff out bribery, fraud, compliance issues, even “potential” litigation – all based on the content of the company’s own documents and data.

kp.k: Conversational research and internal chatbots are anticipated services
kp.d: Miller anticipates plain-English legal research answers drawing on regulations, case law and secondary sources. He also proposes internal FAQ chatbots for legal, HR and compliance queries, with escalation to a lawyer. These statements concern forthcoming or possible functionality rather than demonstrated service quality.
qs: An answer that includes research of regulations, case law, secondary sources, etc.

Moreover, it may be possible to use AI as a “talking” FAQ service (chatbot) that can answer basic legal, HR, and compliance questions from your in-house clients, yet be “smart” enough to know when to defer the answer to a live attorney.

kp.k: Implementation costs and returns depend on organizational circumstances
kp.d: Reporting Rhys Dipshan’s account of Cisco at the 2017 Legalweek Conference, Miller cites an estimated $250,000 for 500 users plus two-and-a-half internal full-time employees to implement a basic virtual-assistant and contracting system. He says ROI depends on tools, customization and user numbers, and predicts falling costs as adoption and computing power increase.
qs: Cisco estimated the cost for 500 users to be around $250,000 plus the need to hire two-and-a-half full-time employees internally to implement the tools for a basic system.
The ROI of AI will be heavily fact-dependent for each organization based on what AI tools the department wants to utilize, the amount of customization needed, the number of users, and so forth.

kp.k: Employment shifts toward engineering, review and higher-value advice
kp.d: Miller predicts elimination of some jobs devoted solely to searching and coding information, alongside new work developing and managing AI, writing algorithms and reviewing AI-assisted output. He expects most lawyers to shift toward analysis and counseling, and asserts that lawyers must retain final responsibility for legal advice.
qs: Jobs will be created, including managing and developing AI (legal engineers), writing algorithms for AI, and reviewing AI-assisted work product (because lawyers can never concede the final say or the provision of legal advice to AI).
Most lawyers will be freed from the mundane task of data gathering for the value-added task of analyzing results, thinking, and advising their clients.

kp.k: Human judgment and relationships underpin the case against substitution
kp.d: Miller reports Matthew Francke’s arguments that clients should not entrust legal advice to computers: advice requires contextual judgment, legal questions lack uniformly clear answers, clients value personal counseling, and lawyers can probe questions framed to obtain a desired answer. These are attributed arguments about enduring human advantages, not empirical findings about technical limits.
qs: Judgment is needed as part of providing any legal advice. Computers cannot do this in the same way humans can.
It’s the personal relationship that cannot be replaced by a computer.
It’s human nature to try to engineer the answer you want to get from a question.

kp.k: Ethical responsibility requires technological understanding and independent legal judgment
kp.d: Miller maintains that lawyers must analyze AI output rather than abdicate responsibility to technology. He quotes Wendy Chang, identified as a member of the ABA’s Standing Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility, linking understanding the technology to ethical compliance and independent judgment. The discussion invokes professional obligations generally without citing specific rule numbers.
qs: Lawyers must still stay involved and, ultimately, take whatever output from AI resources and apply good old-fashioned human legal analysis to come up with the actual legal advice.

In using technology, lawyers must understand the technology that they are using to assure themselves they are doing so in a way that complies with their ethical obligations – and that the advice the client receives is the result of the lawyer’s independent judgment.

kp.k: Holmes illustrates a speculative integrated legal assistant
kp.d: Miller’s imagined desktop assistant, Holmes, combines conversational research, deadline responses, drafting, document retrieval and proactive monitoring of corporate and public information. The scripted exchanges illustrate his desired future capabilities, including reports of possible misconduct and external investigations; they are not accounts of an implemented product or validated outcomes.
qs: My idea (perhaps not that all original) is for a dedicated desktop box and you can ask it complicated legal research and related questions and get useable answers.
It will give you the answer in either spoken form or in an email/Word document.
The first is “basic legal research.”

kp.k: Comprehensive monitoring creates privacy, governance and reliability risks
kp.d: Miller qualifies the Holmes vision with concerns about employee privacy, country-specific legality, information overload, sensitive personal discoveries and misuse by those receiving reports. He also raises correctness, malpractice and drafting-quality questions, anticipating possible changes to professional responsibility codes rather than identifying enacted reforms.
qs: There are employee privacy issues to work through and at a minimum, you’ll need policies to inform employees that information on the company’s servers is subject to search by the company at any time (and even then something like this might not comport with the laws of every country).
Second, you might get overwhelmed with information.
Is there the potential for “malpractice”?
And in terms of drafting, is “good enough” good enough?

kp.k: Adoption should proceed through small pilots and interdisciplinary ownership
kp.d: Miller recommends experimenting with innovative outside counsel at a low cost, appointing an internal AI champion, pursuing continuing education and conferences, choosing one initial departmental use case, and involving an interested IT colleague in procurement and key decisions. These are practical recommendations for gradual adoption rather than an evaluated implementation method.
qs: Find out which of my outside law firms are using AI or intend to use AI and volunteer to be part of any experimental use of the product – in exchange for a low cost point.
Find one use for AI in your legal department and start there.
Make a good friend in your company’s IT department, someone with an interest in AI who can help procure resources and be supportive of Legal’s use of AI.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Miller predicts widespread AI assistance, automation of routine legal tasks, and a shift toward human analysis and counseling, with in-house departments driving substantial market change.
pts.d: Writing in August 2017, Sterling Miller predicts that AI will become an indispensable assistant to practically every lawyer. He argues that AI can address legal departments’ budget and staffing constraints by reducing service costs and freeing lawyers for more involved advice. He describes e-discovery as an existing application that reduces the number of lawyers needed, and presents a mixture of current and forthcoming applications: faster transactional due diligence; standardized, self-service contract preparation; automated contract-data extraction and lifecycle management; legal-spend comparisons supporting negotiations with outside counsel; litigation-outcome prediction; detection of misconduct and potential litigation in company records; and natural-language legal research and basic advisory chatbots. He predicts some elimination of jobs devoted solely to searching and coding information, alongside new work developing and managing AI and reviewing AI-assisted work product. His central model is lawyer augmentation rather than autonomous provision of final legal advice. Separately, his imagined assistant, 'Holmes,' illustrates a prospective system combining research, drafting, monitoring, reporting and delegated actions; it is a vision, not a reported deployment.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article supports its claims primarily through practitioner reasoning, descriptions of applications, linked products and secondary authorities; its concrete implementation-cost example concerns Cisco.
pts.d: Miller describes the progression of e-discovery from keyword searching through deduplication and email threading to predictive coding as an example of time and labor savings. He links to products and articles for the proposed applications, but the supplied text does not provide controlled comparisons, quantified accuracy tests, adoption statistics, or measured employment effects. His claim that in-house departments will be especially influential rests on their stronger incentive to reduce costs relative to law firms billing for time. For implementation costs, Miller relays Rhys Dipshan’s reporting about Cisco: approximately $250,000 for 500 users plus two-and-a-half internal full-time employees for a basic implementation. This is an organization-specific example, not an industry-wide estimate. His expectation of falling costs invokes adoption and Moore’s Law, without a quantified forecast. He draws on Matthew Francke’s arguments about human judgment and client relationships and quotes Wendy Chang on ethical obligations; these are supporting authorities in Miller’s argument, not interviews establishing measured outcomes. The Holmes dialogues are hypothetical illustrations rather than empirical evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Miller distinguishes applications available in 2017 from near-term possibilities and an undated future vision, while making benefits conditional on implementation choices, human judgment and governance.
pts.d: The article describes legal AI as early in its development but on the cusp of widespread adoption. E-discovery and several contracting, analytics and detection functions are presented as already available; the application list explicitly mixes existing and forthcoming capabilities. Natural-language research is described as coming soon, and Miller is expressly uncertain whether fact-based litigation prediction is already possible or will soon become possible. He gives no date for ubiquitous adoption or for the arrival of Holmes. He predicts costs will fall substantially as adoption increases but qualifies ROI by tool selection, customization and user numbers. His labor forecast distinguishes routine information-processing work from judgment, analysis and personal counseling, which he regards as enduring human functions. He insists that lawyers retain final responsibility and apply independent legal analysis to AI output. For extensive monitoring and research, he flags employee privacy, differing national laws, information overload, handling sensitive information, accuracy, malpractice and drafting quality, and anticipates possible changes to professional-responsibility guidance.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal beneficiaries are corporate legal departments and their business clients; routine legal workers and outside counsel face changing demand, while new technical and review roles emerge.
pts.d: Miller’s focus is the corporate buyer side, not unmet civil legal need or access to justice. In-house counsel gain capacity for substantive advice and tools to control external spending, while internal business clients can obtain standardized contracts through self-service and potentially receive basic answers through chatbots that defer to lawyers when necessary. Outside law firms face reduced demand for labor-intensive discovery and diligence and more informed scrutiny of billing rates and efficiency. Workers whose entire role is searching and coding information are identified as particularly exposed to displacement; Miller does not supply headcount forecasts. Legal engineers, algorithm developers and reviewers of AI-assisted work are identified as potential growth roles, with human verification and independent judgment remaining necessary. Companies may benefit from earlier detection of compliance problems, while employees are affected by expanded monitoring and privacy risks. Implementation also creates demand for internal technical support, as illustrated by the Cisco staffing example.
